_doc: The drives between the Office and the cases. Schema: docs/content-format.md, 'The road'. February 1994: snow chains, pay phones, CB, a 1983 Buick Estate wagon.

stops.name: Gassaway
stops.text: The wagon rolls out of Sutton past the courthouse and the Elk, the heater ticking and the back seat full of film cans. Gassaway is the last town where anyone will know the Office by name.
stops.highway: I-79 south
stops.back: WV-4 along the Elk River
stops.sights: Ice on the Elk, a coal train idling at the Gassaway yard, somebody's wash frozen stiff on the line.

stops.name: Clay County
stops.text: The interstate climbs through cut rock and bare hickory; the back road drops into Clay and follows the Elk past trailers and a one-lane bridge. There is no station on the dial for ten miles either way.
stops.highway: I-79 south past Big Otter
stops.back: US-119 through Clay
stops.sights: A hand-lettered sign for ramps that will not be up for two months, and a church with the steeple leaning toward the river.

stops.name: Charleston
stops.text: The gold dome of the capitol comes up out of the Kanawha fog like something that belongs in a bigger state. The interstate stacks through town on concrete legs; the old road goes east up the gorge, where a sign promises a hole where gravity went wrong.
stops.highway: I-77 and I-64 through Charleston
stops.back: US-60 up the Kanawha toward Ansted
stops.sights: The capitol dome, a chemical plant breathing white, and a billboard for the Mystery Hole, SEE IT TO BELIEVE IT.

stops.name: Winfield
stops.text: Past Teays Valley the four lanes end and US-35 turns into two, following the Kanawha north between coal tipples and bottomland. The truckers call it Bloody 35 and the crosses in the ditch say why.
stops.highway: US-35 north
stops.back: WV-62 along the Kanawha
stops.sights: A tipple with its lights on, a white cross with plastic flowers, and the first streaks of river fog crossing the road.

stops.name: The Ohio approach
stops.text: The Kanawha widens, the fog thickens, and the road runs out of hills. Somewhere ahead the river meets the Ohio and the lights of Point Pleasant hang over the water where the Silver Bridge used to be.
stops.highway: US-35 to the Henderson bridge
stops.back: WV-2 along the river
stops.sights: Barge lights on the Kanawha, the Henderson bridge railings coated in ice, and the floodwall at Point Pleasant like a grey shoulder turned to the water.

stops.name: Henderson
stops.text: The wagon crosses the Kanawha with the case boxes rattling in the back and the floodwall shrinking in the mirror. Bloody 35 is worse going south; the fog comes up off the river in the dark and the trucks run it anyway.
stops.highway: US-35 south
stops.back: WV-2 down the river to Buffalo
stops.sights: The power plant stacks blinking red across the Ohio, a towboat pushing coal in the dark, and a pair of headlights that keep the same distance.

stops.name: Teays Valley
stops.text: The two lanes become four again at the interstate and the whole car breathes out. Charleston's glow sits on the clouds ahead and somebody mentions the pie case in Gassaway.
stops.highway: I-64 east into Charleston
stops.back: WV-62 up the Kanawha through Winfield
stops.sights: A Go-Mart lit like a landing strip, a flatbed of pipe, the Kanawha running black and fast under the Winfield bridge.

stops.name: Elkview
stops.text: North of Charleston the interstate empties out and climbs back into the hills. It is a long dark pull to Sutton with the heater on low to save gas, and everyone in the car is thinking about the filing.
stops.highway: I-79 north
stops.back: WV-4 up the Elk through Clay
stops.sights: Elkview's one stoplight blinking yellow, the river under ice, and the Braxton County line sign shot through with birdshot.

sutton_to_sandown.name: Sutton to Sandown
sutton_to_sandown.arrive_day: You come into %s station on a two-carriage train older than the Office, into bunting and gulls.
sutton_to_sandown.arrive_night: You come into %s after dark. The last train empties and the sea is somewhere to the left, loud. Dread rises.

stops.name: Gassaway
stops.text: For once the wagon turns north. The windows are down because the heater is stuck on, the passports are in a coffee can on the dash, and the back seat is tape stock, a suitcase each and a map of an island smaller than Braxton County. Gassaway's on-ramp is the last place anyone waves.
stops.highway: I-79 north to Morgantown, then I-68 east over the mountains
stops.back: US-19 north through Weston and Clarksburg
stops.sights: The Elk low and brown, hay down in the bottoms, a boy selling nightcrawlers off a card table, and the courthouse clock in Sutton already wrong behind you.

stops.name: Cumberland, Maryland
stops.text: I-68 comes down off Big Savage Mountain into the Narrows, a slot in the ridge barely wide enough for the river, the railroad and the road. Cumberland sits in the bottom of it with church spires and a dead Kelly-Springfield plant. From here it is the Beltway, the airport, and the car in a lot for a week.
stops.highway: I-68 east through the Narrows, I-70 and I-270 to the Beltway
stops.back: US-40, the National Road, over Sideling Hill to Hancock
stops.sights: The Sideling Hill road cut with its rock folded like a sandwich, a Western Maryland caboose on a siding, and the first Washington plates with their hoods up in the heat.

stops.name: Dulles
stops.text: The Buick goes into economy parking under a sign that says REMEMBER YOUR ROW, and nobody does. The terminal is a concrete wing on a hill and the mobile lounges drive you out to the plane like a bus going somewhere unusual. Eight hours. The ocean, then England.
stops.highway: The overnight flight to Heathrow
stops.sights: The lounge window full of a 747's belly, a sunset over Virginia at the wrong angle, and a man across the aisle reading a paperback about Loch Ness with the cover folded back.

stops.name: Heathrow
stops.text: Morning, English and grey, and everyone talks like the BBC except faster. The Piccadilly line takes you in from under the airport, the Bakerloo drops you at Waterloo, and a slam-door train for Portsmouth Harbour sits at platform twelve with its windows open. The cases go up on the luggage rack and stay there.
stops.highway: The Piccadilly line in, the Bakerloo to Waterloo, then the Portsmouth Harbour train
stops.sights: Back gardens with washing out, a cricket pitch nobody is using, Guildford cathedral on its hill, and a hedge that does not stop for forty miles.

stops.name: Portsmouth Harbour
stops.text: The train stops at the end of a pier with the harbour on three sides and the Isle of Wight lying across the water like a long grey animal asleep. A hovercraft sits on the slip with its skirt deflated, looking like something a child drew. Beside it a car ferry loads for Fishbourne with a queue of Vauxhalls and a coach from Birmingham.
stops.highway: Across the Solent to the island
stops.sights: HMS Victory's masts over a dockyard wall, the Spinnaker-less skyline of 1994, a Sealink ferry backing out with a long honk, and the hovercraft fans starting up like a storm indoors.

choices.text: The car ferry to Fishbourne, then a bus

stops.name: Ryde Pier Head
stops.text: The island train waits at the end of half a mile of pier: two red carriages built for the London Underground in 1938, bought second-hand in 1989, with the Northern line still printed on the route map above the seats. It rattles down the pier over the water, through Ryde's tunnel, and out into fields.
stops.highway: The Island Line down the pier and through Brading
stops.sights: The pier boards passing under the carriage floor, Ryde esplanade with its boating lake, a Portsmouth skyline shrinking across the Solent, and sheep looking up at a tube train.

stops.name: Brading
stops.text: Brading is a signal box, a bridge and a platform where nobody gets on. South of it the land flattens into reeds and ditches, Brading Marsh, with Culver Down's white cliff standing at the end of it like a wall. The next stop is Sandown. The carriage goes quiet without anybody deciding to.
stops.highway: The last stretch of the Island Line into Sandown
stops.sights: Reed beds laid flat by the wind, a heron that does not move, the old Bembridge branch going off into brambles, and a yellow something on a fence post that is gone before anyone can say what it was.

sandown_to_sutton.name: Sandown to Sutton
sandown_to_sutton.arrive_day: You come into %s with the windows down, past the courthouse, and the Office looks small and exactly where you left it.
sandown_to_sutton.arrive_night: You come into %s after midnight with the Buick ticking and the courthouse clock wrong. The Office is dark. Dread rises.

stops.name: Sandown station
stops.text: The case boxes go up on the rack of a 1938 carriage and Sandown slides away: the bay, the pier, the bunting that was up when you came. Brading Marsh, Ryde tunnel, the long pier out over the water, and the hovercraft waiting on the slip with its fans already turning.
stops.highway: The Island Line to Ryde and the hovercraft to Portsmouth
stops.sights: Culver Down going behind the houses, a man on the pier with a telescope pointed at nothing, and the island turning back into a shape across the Solent.

stops.name: Portsmouth Harbour
stops.text: The Waterloo train is a slow one with every window open and a carriage of sailors going on leave. London, the Bakerloo, the Piccadilly, and Heathrow's tunnels, with the evidence bags in the hand luggage and a story ready for customs about a fossil.
stops.highway: The train to Waterloo and the tube to Heathrow
stops.sights: The same hedge the other way, Guildford's cathedral, a cricket match this time with eleven men in white standing very still, and Big Ben from the Waterloo platforms for anyone who leans.

stops.name: Heathrow
stops.text: The day flight home, chasing the sun west so the afternoon lasts eleven hours. A cold lunch on a tray, a film nobody watches, and the Atlantic going by underneath like a floor. Everyone in the party is already arguing the verdict in their head.
stops.highway: The day flight to Dulles
stops.sights: Ireland green under broken cloud, then nothing but water and the plane's own shadow, then Newfoundland with snow still in the folds in May.

stops.name: Dulles
stops.text: The Buick is where it was, under a week of pollen, and starts on the third try. Out past the Beltway the evening comes down over Maryland and the mountains start again at Hancock. It is a long pull west with the island still in everyone's ears and the sorting room waiting.
stops.highway: I-270 and I-68 west over the mountains, then I-79 south
stops.back: US-50 west through Romney and Grafton to Clarksburg
stops.sights: The Sideling Hill cut lit orange, the Narrows at dusk with a coal train in it, and a pair of headlights that keep the same distance.

sutton_to_kelly.name: Sutton to Kelly
sutton_to_kelly.arrive_day: You come into %s on 41 with the windows down, past the tobacco warehouses and the stockyard smell, and park on the courthouse square under a Greyhound sign that has not had a bus under it all day.
sutton_to_kelly.arrive_night: You come into %s after dark. The courthouse clock is lit, the square is empty, and the Greyhound sign buzzes over a bench with nobody on it. For the last ten miles something in the hedgerows along 41 kept pace with the headlights. Dread rises.

stops.name: Gassaway
stops.text: August, and the wagon pulls out of Sutton with every window down because the heater is stuck on and has been since February. The back seat is tape stock, two coolers and a box of Kelly clippings from 1955 that Ruth will not let anyone sit on. Gassaway's on-ramp shimmers. Nine hours by the interstates, twelve by the back roads, and the Buick's gas gauge is already arguing with itself.
stops.highway: I-79 south to Charleston
stops.back: WV-4 down the Elk through Clay and Clendenin
stops.sights: The Elk low and green between its rocks, a boy on a bridge rail with a cane pole, Queen Anne's lace in the ditches, and the courthouse clock in Sutton wrong behind you as always.

stops.name: Charleston
stops.text: The capitol dome comes up gold over the Kanawha in a haze you can taste. I-64 west takes the river's north bank on concrete stilts past the chemical plants, each with its own weather. The back road is US-60 along the water, through St. Albans and Nitro, where every third building was something to do with the war once.
stops.highway: I-64 west through Charleston and Teays Valley
stops.back: US-60 down the Kanawha through St. Albans and Hurricane
stops.sights: The capitol dome, a chemical plant breathing white into a white sky, a towboat pushing nine barges of coal downriver, and a billboard for a Sternwheel Regatta that was last month.

stops.name: The Ohio crossing
stops.text: Huntington is brick and rail yards and a river that is suddenly the Ohio, wide and brown and slow. The interstate jumps the Big Sandy into Kentucky without ceremony; the back road is US-60 through Ashland, past the Armco stacks and the steel town's Saturday faces. Somewhere in the middle of the bridge the car is in a different state and nobody says anything.
stops.highway: I-64 west over the Big Sandy into Kentucky
stops.back: US-60 through Huntington and Ashland along the river
stops.sights: Marshall's green roofs, the Ashland steelworks with one stack going, a barge tow longer than the bridge, and thunderheads building over Ohio like a second range of hills.

stops.name: Mount Sterling
stops.text: The hills give out past Morehead and the land goes to pasture, limestone and white plank fence. Horse country, with the fences running for miles and the barns painted better than the houses. Lexington sits on the interstate like a city that expects you; the back road is US-60 through Mount Sterling and Winchester, the Bluegrass Parkway's poorer cousin, two lanes and tobacco on either side.
stops.highway: I-64 west past Lexington
stops.back: US-60 through Mount Sterling and Winchester, the old road
stops.sights: White fences to the horizon, a yearling standing in the shade of one tree, a sign for a bourbon distillery tour, and the first tobacco cut and speared in the field.

stops.name: Elizabethtown
stops.text: The Bluegrass Parkway runs out at Elizabethtown and the Western Kentucky Parkway takes over, a toll road with the tolls recently gone and the booths still standing. Bowling Green is an hour south with a Corvette plant and a museum nearly built. The back road drops through Leitchfield into caves country, where the ground is hollow and every farm has a sinkhole it does not talk about.
stops.highway: The Western Kentucky Parkway west from Elizabethtown
stops.back: KY-259 through Leitchfield and the caves country
stops.sights: An empty toll booth with a wasp nest in it, a Fort Knox tank on a flatbed, a hand-lettered sign for a cave tour, and heat lightning in the south with no thunder behind it.

stops.name: Pembroke
stops.text: The Pennyrile Parkway brings you down to US-41 on the far side of Hopkinsville and the last leg is the old road in. Tobacco barns start, black and slatted, smoke coming out of the eaves where the dark-fired crop is curing. Fort Campbell's traffic shares the road: pickups with post stickers, a Humvee, a bus full of soldiers with their heads against the glass. Kelly is a crossroads eight miles up 41 and nobody wants to pass it first in the dark.
stops.highway: US-41 north into Hopkinsville
stops.back: The Fairview road past the Jefferson Davis obelisk, then in by Pembroke
stops.sights: Tobacco barns smoking in the heat, a 351-foot concrete obelisk standing in a cornfield for no reason anyone can explain, a Fort Campbell bus, and a stretch of hedgerow where the cicadas stop.

kelly_to_sutton.name: Kelly to Sutton
kelly_to_sutton.arrive_day: You come into %s late in the afternoon with the windows down and Kentucky dust on everything, past the courthouse, and the Office looks small and exactly where you left it.
kelly_to_sutton.arrive_night: You come into %s after midnight with the Buick ticking and the courthouse clock wrong. The Office is dark. Nobody has slept properly in days. Dread rises.

stops.name: Hopkinsville
stops.text: The case boxes go in the back, the coolers go in empty, and the wagon pulls off the courthouse square with the Greyhound sign in the mirror. Nobody looks at the Kelly turn as 41 goes past it. The Pennyrile Parkway north is empty and straight and the heat is already up at eight in the morning. It is a long way home and everyone in the car is tired in a way sleep has not fixed.
stops.highway: The Pennyrile Parkway north to the Western Kentucky Parkway
stops.back: US-41 north through Crofton and Madisonville
stops.sights: Tobacco barns smoking, a Fort Campbell convoy going the other way, a sinkhole pond with a dead tree standing in it, and the sign for Kelly going by without anyone reading it out.

stops.name: Elizabethtown
stops.text: The Western Kentucky Parkway runs east through the knobs with the heat haze lying on it like water. Elizabethtown is gas, coffee and a payphone. The back road is US-62 through Leitchfield, slower and shaded, with the caves country under it and the cicadas going like a bearing about to fail.
stops.highway: The Western Kentucky Parkway east, then the Bluegrass Parkway
stops.back: US-62 through Leitchfield and the knobs
stops.sights: An empty toll booth, a Fort Knox tank on a flatbed going the other way now, a drive-in with the screen holed by weather, and a sky in the east the colour of a bruise.

stops.name: Lexington
stops.text: Horse country again, the white fences running for miles and nobody in the car saying anything about them this time. Lexington on the interstate, then the long easy grade toward Winchester and the hills. The back road is US-60 through Mount Sterling, the old road, with the tobacco mostly cut now and hanging in the barns.
stops.highway: I-64 east past Lexington toward Morehead
stops.back: US-60 through Winchester and Mount Sterling
stops.sights: White fences, a horse van with its ramp down in a gateway, a bourbon warehouse black with the angels' share, and a pair of headlights that keep the same distance.

stops.name: The Ohio crossing
stops.text: The sky over Ohio has been building all afternoon and it breaks at the river. The Big Sandy bridge in rain, Huntington's rail yards steaming, the wipers losing. Then West Virginia, Charleston's dome in the wet dusk, and I-79 north through the hills in the dark with the case boxes shifting on the curves and the sorting room waiting.
stops.highway: I-64 east over the Big Sandy, then I-79 north from Charleston
stops.back: US-60 through Ashland and Huntington, then WV-4 up the Elk
stops.sights: Lightning walking down the Ohio, the Ashland stacks lit by it, a towboat holding station mid-river with its searchlight on the water, and the Braxton County line sign in the headlights at last.

hitchhiker.title: A hitchhiker with a guitar case
hitchhiker.text: A man in an army coat stands at the end of a gravel drive with a guitar case at his feet and his thumb out, not hopeful, just out. The case has a Point Pleasant Regatta sticker on it, years old. He does not wave the wagon down; he waits to see what it does.

options.line: He folds into the back with the case across his knees and talks for forty miles. Somewhere past the county line he plays three chords of something about the river, and Teddy writes the words on the back of a map. His cousin is a deputy in Mason County and has a story about a grey bird.
Home, he says, if it's still there. He names the town before you do and gives you a street and a name to ask for, and then says no to the ride after all. He'd rather walk it.

fail.line: He looks at the Office lettering on the door and the thumb comes down. 'I've talked to your kind,' he says, and picks up the case.

options.line: He gets smaller in the mirror and does not watch you go.

pie_diner.title: A diner with a pie case
pie_diner.text: A diner sits in a gravel lot under a sign that just says EAT, its windows fogged from the inside. A rotating pie case turns slowly on the counter: coconut cream, apple, something red. The cook has a Point Pleasant Black Knights jacket hanging on the coat rack.

options.line: Pie, coffee, eggs, the works, and the heater vent under the booth. For twenty minutes nobody talks about the case and it is the best thing that happens all day.

options.text: Ask the cook about the sightings
options.line: He wipes the counter around your cup while he tells it. 'Half of that in '66 was Kessler's boys with a reflector on a stick,' he says, 'and the other half nobody can tell you.' He says it like a man who has told both halves.
Two paper cups and a lid that will not seal. It is still the only warm thing in the car.

breakdown.title: Breakdown on the shoulder
breakdown.text: The wagon coughs twice, catches, then dies on a stretch of road with a ditch on one side and a guardrail on the other. The dash lights stay on. Outside it is cold enough that the breath in the car fogs the windshield within a minute.

options.line: Fuel line, iced at the bend. A rag, a lighter and a cold ten minutes get it running, and Frank says the Buick has done this to him twice.

fail.line: An hour under the hood with a flashlight in your teeth finds nothing. A pulpwood truck finally stops and tows the wagon to a garage that charges by the quarter hour.

options.text: Call for help on the CB
options.line: Channel 19 answers on the second try. A tanker driver named Pigeon pulls over twenty minutes later with jumper cables and a thermos and will not take money for it.
The phone is two miles back at a closed store. The wrecker takes an hour to come and another to find a shop that is open, and the driver talks about Point Pleasant the whole way.

mystery_hole.title: The Mystery Hole
mystery_hole.text: A gorilla statue and a VW Beetle nosed into the roof mark the Mystery Hole, Ansted, open since 1973, where the signs say the laws of nature do not apply. A woman in a parka takes dollars at a window. Inside, by all accounts, water runs uphill and a ball rolls the wrong way.

options.line: The floor is tilted and so is everything on it, and your inner ear argues with your eyes for fifteen minutes. On the way out there is a rack of postcards printed on the slant. Teddy says it's the most honest place in the state: it tells you it is a trick and you still feel it.

options.text: Work out the trick from the parking lot
options.line: The building leans eleven degrees into the hill and the roofline hides it. A tilted room with a level floor painted on the wall, and your body believes the wall. You say so, and nobody is less tempted.

fail.line: You stand in the lot looking at a crooked building for ten minutes and end up less sure than when you arrived. Frank pays for a postcard just to annoy you.

options.line: The gorilla watches you go. Somebody in the back seat says 'next time' and means it.

lights_over_field.title: Lights in the sky over a field
lights_over_field.text: Three lights hang over a bottomland field, orange, steady, in a line too level for anything on a wing. They do not blink. A farmhouse at the far end of the field has every light on.

options.line: Six frames at a long exposure with the camera on the roof of the wagon. The lights go out one at a time, left to right, while the shutter is open on the last one. Nobody says anything until the car is moving.
They hold for four minutes by the dash clock, then go out together. The farmhouse lights stay on. Nobody comes to the door.
Flares, says Frank. Nobody argues, and nobody looks in the mirror.

deer_then_something.title: A deer, then something else, in the headlights
deer_then_something.text: A doe steps into the cone of the headlights and stands with her eyes lit green, and then goes. A second later something else comes out of the brush behind where she was: taller, upright, and gone before the brakes finish squealing. The fog closes over the road.

options.line: The wagon stops crooked across the line and you get out with the flashlight. Tracks in the slush on the shoulder: deer, and then a wide, flat print that is not deer, going toward the river.

fail.line: You stop too late and too hard. The front end kisses the guardrail, a headlight goes, and whatever it was is not there when you look.

options.line: The roof-rack spotlight floods the brush white. Something turns in it, slow, and two red points come back at the car and then are gone. Teddy has to be told to breathe.
The wagon fishtails and catches, and the tail end of the fog bank swallows the road behind you. A deer, you say. Everyone agrees out loud.

black_sedan.title: A black sedan in the mirror
black_sedan.text: A pair of headlights has held the same distance behind the wagon for twenty miles, through two towns and a speed trap, never closer, never gone. When a truck's lights sweep across it there is a black sedan under them, an old one, a model nobody has made since the sixties, polished like it came off the lot. The dash radio hisses three faint notes and stops.

options.line: You kill the headlights at the top of a hill and take the first gravel road without braking. Ten minutes in the dark with the engine off, and the sedan goes by on the main road at exactly the speed it was doing before. It does not slow.

fail.line: You take the gravel road and the sedan takes it too, lights off, the same distance back. When you reach pavement again it is somehow ahead of you, and then it is behind you again.

options.line: You stop on the shoulder and the sedan stops behind you. A man in a dark suit and a hat walks up without a coat in February and stands at the window. 'Mr. Penrose,' he says, as if answering. He asks how the filing went and whether you found the room on the fourth floor, and says the Office was always better at listening than at being right. 'Augusta thought so too.' He walks back to the sedan before anyone can ask who that is, and it pulls out without lighting its lamps.

You drive the speed limit and do not look again. It is still there at the county line. It is still there when you stop for gas, parked across the lot with nobody in it, and it is not there when you come out.

bloody_35_chains.title: Snow on Bloody 35
bloody_35_chains.text: Sleet turns to snow somewhere past Winfield and the two lanes of US-35 go white at once. A coal truck passes doing sixty and throws a wall of slush across the windshield. There is a plow somewhere; it is not here.

options.line: Twenty cold minutes on your knees in the slush, Frank holding the flashlight and swearing in rhythm. After that the wagon goes where it is pointed, and the trucks can do what they like.
Second gear, no brakes, and the ruts left by the trucks. It takes an extra hour and a lot of silence, and it works.

fail.line: The back end lets go on a curve above the river and the wagon ends up nose-down in the ditch, undamaged, immovable. A farmer with a tractor pulls it out for twenty dollars and a lecture about chains.

options.text: Wait it out at a gas station
options.line: A Union 76 with a kerosene heater and a dog. The snow stops after two hours and the plow finally comes through, and the man at the register says it's always like this on 35, that's why the crosses.

fog_bank.title: A fog bank off the river
fog_bank.text: The river fog comes across the road in one piece, a wall, and inside it the headlights show twenty feet of wet asphalt and nothing else. Taillights ahead flare and vanish. Somewhere a truck downshifts and you cannot tell from which direction.

options.line: You tuck in behind a coal truck and drive its red lights for eleven miles, closer than anyone should. It knows the road. When the fog breaks it is just gone, as if it was never there.

fail.line: The truck pulls away and leaves you alone in it. You crawl along at fifteen with the window down to hear the road, and the fog does not lift for an hour.

options.text: Ask on the CB where it ends
options.line: 'Clears at the Buffalo bridge, northbound, and watch for the flatbed at the Red Hill curve.' You take the advice and the flatbed is exactly where he said.
You sit at a church lot with the engine running for warmth and the wipers going on nothing. Two hours. Somebody in the car says they can hear the river, and nobody else can.

truck_stop_cb.title: A truck stop with a CB on the counter
truck_stop_cb.text: A truck stop under sodium lights, diesel pumps on one side and a lunch counter on the other. A CB base station sits by the register with the squelch open, and the drivers talk over each other about weigh stations, the snow north of Ripley, and two men in a black car asking questions at the Mason Gas.

options.line: A driver named Hollowell has it from a dispatcher who has it from a deputy: two men, dark suits, no coats, in February, asking the gas station man what he saw and whether he had told anyone. 'Feds,' says Hollowell. The man next to him says no.

options.text: Buy a set of snow chains
options.line: Behind the counter, next to the fan belts and the Vivarin. Twenty dollars, and the man throws in a pair of cotton gloves because he has seen what people's hands look like after.
Regular, pumped by a kid in a watch cap who does the windshield without being asked. It is the last cheap gas before the river.

bridge_detour.title: A closed bridge and a detour
bridge_detour.text: Orange barrels and a flagman in a reflective vest block the road at a steel truss bridge. The sign says BRIDGE CLOSED, INSPECTION, with a detour arrow pointing up a road with no number. The flagman is drinking coffee from a thermos lid and looks like he has been there since the state built the bridge.

options.line: The detour is eighteen miles of switchbacks through a hollow where every dog comes out to the road. It rejoins the highway at a crossroads with a store that sells gas by the gallon and a lot of nothing else.

options.text: Ask the flagman for a better way
options.line: 'Office, huh. My aunt wrote you people in '68.' He lifts the barrel and waves you across the bridge with the inspectors watching, one car, slow, no stopping.

fail.line: He has been asked that forty times today. He points at the arrow and goes back to his coffee.

options.text: Wait for the inspection to finish
options.line: Three hours in a cold car with the engine on and off, watching men in hard hats walk the trusses. The flagman eventually lets you through without looking up.

state_trooper.title: A state trooper's lights
state_trooper.text: Blue lights come up in the mirror and stay there. A West Virginia State Police cruiser, campaign hat and all, pulls the wagon over on a straight stretch with nothing around but a fence. The trooper walks up slow, looks at the equipment in the back, the antennas, the Office lettering on the door.

options.line: Investigators, Sutton, going to Point Pleasant on a case. He looks at you for a long second and says to watch the fog on 35 and that his sergeant has a file on your Office thicker than his. He does not write anything.

options.text: Tell him you're with the newspaper
options.line: The Gazette, a feature on the anniversary. He loses interest in a way that only a reporter can make happen and waves you off with a warning about the taillight.

fail.line: He asks which editor and you do not have a name. The ticket is for the taillight, the lecture is for the lie, and both take a while.

options.text: Kill the scanner before he reaches the window
options.line: The police scanner goes dark a second before his flashlight finds it. He looks at the box, then at you. 'Keep it off in Mason County,' he says, and lets it go.

church_sign.title: A church sign
church_sign.text: A white frame church with a black letterboard sign out front, the plastic letters pushed in crooked. It reads WHAT WATCHES FROM THE RIVER WATCHES YOU TOO, and under it, REVIVAL FEB 20. The lot is empty and there are tire ruts in the snow going around the back.

options.line: The other side of the sign has last week's message still up, the letters gone grey with weather: HE SAW THE BIRD AND WAS NOT AFRAID. Isaiah does not say that. Somebody here wrote their own verse.

fail.line: The other side is bare except for three letters nobody took down: G, U, S. It means nothing and it stays with you for miles.

options.line: Frank reads it aloud in a preacher voice and Teddy does not laugh.

low_water_crossing.title: A flooded low-water crossing
low_water_crossing.text: The back road drops to a concrete ford across a creek, and the creek is up: brown water running fast over the slab with a depth gauge on a post that reads somewhere between one foot and two. Ice rims the banks. Someone has tied a red rag to the gauge, which could mean anything.

options.line: Low gear, steady throttle, upstream side of the slab where the water is shallowest. The wagon pushes a bow wave to the far bank and climbs out dripping.

fail.line: Halfway across the engine drowns. You sit in the dark with the water sucking at the doors until a man with a tractor and a chain pulls you out backward and will not take less than fifteen dollars.

options.text: Wade out and check the depth
options.line: Knee-deep and rising, but the slab is sound and the current is on the downstream edge. You walk the line and then drive it, and the only thing lost is an hour and the feeling in your feet.
Back up the hill and around by the county road, twelve miles the long way. The creek will still be up tomorrow.

motel_night.title: A motel sign in the dark
motel_night.text: A motor court with half its neon working, VACANCY in pink, the office lit by a television. Eight rooms in a row with a car in front of one. It is late, the road is long, and the driver has started blinking slower than is safe.

options.line: Twenty-two dollars for two beds, a cot, a heater that bangs and a shower with pressure. You sleep like the dead and dream about nothing, which is the best you can hope for on this road.

options.text: Sleep on the mattress in the back
options.line: Seats down, the mattress in, coats for blankets and the engine run ten minutes an hour for the heater. It is not a bed. It is free, and nobody has to sign a register.
Coffee from the thermos and the window cracked for the cold. The road keeps coming and the mind starts to put things in the ditches that are not there.

payphone.title: A pay phone outside a closed store
payphone.text: A pay phone bolted to the wall of a cinderblock store that closed at six, its light the only one for a mile. The receiver is cold enough to stick to an ear. There is a phone book on a chain with the cover torn off.

options.line: The answering machine in the sorting room picks up after four rings and you listen to your own voice tell you nobody is in. You leave the stop and the time anyway, because that is the rule, and feel better for it.

Directory assistance, a quarter, and the Lowe Hotel's night clerk, who says there is a room if you get there before eleven and that the fourth floor is closed, don't ask. The line clicks twice before you hang up.
Nobody to call who would answer. You get back in the car.

jet_lag.title: Jet lag over the Atlantic
jet_lag.text: The cabin lights go down somewhere past Newfoundland and the plane settles into the long hum. Five time zones are going to land on the party at once in the morning. The case file is in the seat pocket. The pillow is the size of a sandwich.

options.line: Coat over the head, shoes off, the engine note for a lullaby. It is not good sleep but it is six hours of it, and the island will get a party that can stand up straight.

The reading light makes a small room out of the seat. Two children, a meadow, a man in a pointed hat who said he came from somewhere else. By the time the breakfast trolley comes you know every name in the file and the sun is up over Ireland and it feels like three in the morning, because it is.

first_british_things.title: The first British things
first_british_things.text: Everything is slightly the wrong size. The train is narrow, the doors have handles on the outside, the money is heavy and the coins have a woman on them. A man opposite reads a newspaper with a page three that Teddy looks at twice. Somebody says 'cheers' for no reason anyone can find.

options.text: Ask the man opposite about the Isle of Wight
options.line: He folds the paper. 'Sandown? Bucket and spade. My nan went every year.' He says there is a zoo with tigers, a pier, and that the marsh behind the town floods, and he asks what Americans want with it. 'A story about a yellow man,' you say, and his face changes. He heard it on the radio.

fail.line: He looks over the paper, says 'Can't help you, mate,' and goes back to it. Nobody on the carriage meets anyone's eye for the next forty miles. It is apparently a rule.

options.line: A sandwich in a triangular box, a cup of tea with the bag still in it, and a chocolate bar whose name sounds like a town. The tea is the best thing that has happened since Dulles.
Brick, hedge, chimney, hedge. Everything is older than everything at home and nobody on the train has noticed. The sky is the same low grey as Sutton in March and somehow warmer.

hovercraft_passenger.title: The woman on the hovercraft
hovercraft_passenger.text: The hovercraft lifts, roars and goes out over the Solent like a bus skating on a lake, and the woman in the next seat holds the rail with both hands. She is fifty, maybe, in a good coat with a badge pinned to the lapel: an enamel sun, SUNNYSIDE HOLIDAY CAMP, 1973. She sees you looking at it.

options.line: 'Redcoat. Well, Yellowcoat; Sunnyside did it yellow.' She was an entertainer that season, the summer the children saw something on the marsh, and she has not been back to the island since. 'I'm going to see the camp before they knock it down.' She writes a name on your ticket. 'If you're asking about that summer, ask for me.'

options.text: Say you are going to Sandown about 1973
options.line: She does not ask how you know. 'They laughed at those kids,' she says, 'and some of us didn't, and that cost.' One of the camp's entertainers left mid-season and never wrote. She gives you her name and a guest house, and does not let go of the rail until Ryde.

fail.line: Her face closes like a door. 'Lot of people went to Sandown in 1973.' She moves to a seat across the aisle and watches the water for the rest of the crossing. The badge stays on.

options.line: Ten minutes of spray on the windows and the island coming up out of it, a long pier, a church on a hill. When you look back her seat is empty and the badge is on it, left or dropped, and then the crew are shouting for everyone to stay seated until the skirt is down.

ferry_crossing.title: The slow way over
ferry_crossing.text: The car ferry takes forty minutes to cross what the hovercraft does in ten, and the party spends it on the open deck with a coach party from Birmingham, a flask being passed round and the sea the colour of slate. At Fishbourne there is a bus, eventually.

options.line: They are going to Sandown for the week, every year since 1961, and the driver remembers 1973 because the marsh flooded and the camp cancelled the Saturday show. 'Something about the kiddies seeing a man in a hat.' He laughs, and then does not.
A bench in the lounge, the engine coming up through it, and twenty minutes of nothing. The bus at Fishbourne is late and the driver sings.
Spray, gulls, the island getting bigger. Nothing happens, which after the week this has been is a thing in itself.

marsh_from_train.title: The marsh from the train
marsh_from_train.text: South of Brading the train runs on an embankment with the marsh on both sides, reeds to the horizon and the white end of Culver Down standing over it. In the middle of the reeds there is a patch of bare ground, round, where nothing grows, and a stile with a path to it. A child in the carriage says 'Look' and nobody looks but you.

options.line: A church spire to the left, the cliff to the right, the stile between: three lines on the Ordnance Survey sheet cross on a meadow by a brook. You have the place before you have the town.

fail.line: By the time the map is out the train has curved and the reeds all look the same. Teddy says it was on the left. It was on the right.

options.text: Ask the child what they saw
options.line: 'A man.' The mother says there was nobody there, love, and the child says 'He was yellow,' and the mother says that's enough. The child does not look out of the window again all the way to Sandown.
You watch the other side of the carriage, where there is a golf course and a man in a tank top missing a putt. Whatever is on the marsh will keep until tomorrow. It has kept since 1973.

suits_on_the_plane.title: A grey suit two rows ahead
suits_on_the_plane.text: Somewhere over the Atlantic you notice that the man two rows ahead on the aisle is reading a manila folder with an Office stamp on the tab. Your case file. The one in your bag, which is still in your bag. He has it open on the tray table, upside down, turning the pages at reading speed. His hat is in the overhead locker. He has not had a drink.

options.text: Walk up the aisle and look
options.line: You stand at his shoulder as if waiting for the toilet. It is your handwriting, your photographs, the verdict page blank. He does not look up. 'Hoax travels better,' he says, pleasantly, to the folder. 'Lighter. Nothing to declare.' When you get back to your seat the folder is in your bag and the man is asleep with his hands folded.

fail.line: Halfway up the aisle the seatbelt sign chimes and a steward steers you back. When the plane levels out the seat two rows ahead is empty and the folder in your bag is warm, as if it has been in the sun.

options.line: He reads to the end, closes it, and sits with his hands on it for an hour. When the meal comes he waves it away. When the lights go down he is still sitting straight. When they come up for landing the seat is empty and the steward says it was empty the whole flight.

options.text: Pull the shade down and sleep
options.line: You decide not to have seen it, and sleep like a stone until the wheels come down over Virginia. In your bag the folder is in order. Someone has filled in the verdict page in pencil, lightly, and rubbed it out.

fruit_stand.title: A fruit stand under a tarp
fruit_stand.text: A pickup backed up to the shoulder with its tailgate down and a blue tarp over it, a hand-lettered sign: PEACHES, TOMATOES, HONEY. A woman in a lawn chair fans herself with a seed catalogue. It is the first real heat of the year and the wagon's heater is stuck on.

options.line: Soft, warm from the sun, eaten over the dash with the juice running. She throws in a jar of honey because 'you all look like you're going somewhere.' You are.

options.text: Ask her if anything odd comes through here
options.line: She thinks about it with the fan going. 'Black car, every so often. Old. Never stops, never buys.' She says it like weather. 'Goes north. Comes back south about a week after.'
The tarp flaps in the mirror and then the road bends and takes it.

maryland_trooper.title: A trooper on the mountain
maryland_trooper.text: A Maryland State Police cruiser sits in the median at the top of a grade with its radar out the window. It comes out behind the wagon as you pass and the lights come on a mile later, on a stretch with a runaway-truck ramp and a view of three states. The trooper walks up slow, looks at the West Virginia plates, the antennas, the Office lettering on the door.

options.line: Investigators, Sutton, headed for the airport and a case in England. He says 'England' the way you would say 'the moon', writes nothing, and tells you the Beltway is a parking lot after three. He is right.

options.text: Tell him you're a film crew
options.line: Documentary, the National Road, public television. He asks which station and you name the one in Morgantown. He loses interest at once and waves you off with a warning about the speed through the Narrows.

fail.line: He asks which station and you say the wrong one. The ticket is for seventy-four in a sixty-five, the lecture is about honesty, and both take a while in the heat.

options.text: Kill the scanner before he reaches the window
options.line: The scanner goes dark a second before his hand finds the door. He looks at the box, then at you. 'Maryland doesn't like those,' he says, and lets it go.

beltway_crawl.title: The Beltway
beltway_crawl.text: Eight lanes of Washington going nowhere at four miles an hour, every car with the windows up and the air on, and the Buick with its windows down and the heater on. A sign for Dulles promises eleven miles. The gas gauge says it will be a near thing. A man in the next lane is shaving.

options.line: An hour and ten minutes to go eleven miles, with the radio for company and Frank reading the names of the exits aloud as if they were places. Somewhere near Tysons the car in front has a bumper sticker that says I BRAKE FOR MOTHMAN and Teddy wants to get out and ask.

options.text: Cut across on the surface streets
options.line: Off at the next exit, a map on the steering wheel, and forty minutes of Virginia subdivisions with names like plantations. You come out on the airport road ahead of the traffic you left.

fail.line: Every surface street in Virginia goes to a cul-de-sac. You are back on the Beltway two exits behind where you got off, and the man is still shaving.

options.text: Pull off for gas and let it clear
options.line: A station with a lot you can sleep in, coffee, and the tank filled against whatever is waiting on the far side of the ocean. When you come back the road is moving.

tea_trolley.title: The tea trolley
tea_trolley.text: A trolley comes down the aisle with a hiss of urn and a rattle of crisps, pushed by a woman who has seen everything a train can contain. Tea, coffee, something called a Kit Kat, a sandwich that was made in a factory on purpose. 'Hot drinks, cold drinks, snacks.'

options.line: Four teas in cups with lids that do not fit, milk already in, and a biscuit each. It costs nothing like what it should and it is, everyone agrees quietly, the finest beverage of the trip.

She does the Portsmouth run four times a day and says half of Birmingham is on the island this weekend. 'And the papers are on about Sandown. Some yellow fella on the golf links. Don't mind that. Mind the gulls, they'll have your chips.'
She moves on. The hiss of the urn goes down the carriage and out of it, and the party goes back to looking at hedges.

ticket_inspector.title: Tickets, please
ticket_inspector.text: A man in a British Rail waistcoat with a leather satchel and a clipper comes through the carriage saying 'Tickets, please' in the tone of a man who has said it a hundred thousand times. He looks at the party's tickets, then at the party, then at the equipment cases on the rack.

options.line: He clips four tickets, glances at the Office lettering on the tape case, and says 'Sandown, change at Ryde.' Then, half turning back: 'You'll be the Americans. There's a bloke on the pier been asking if you've come.' He does not say which bloke.

options.text: Ask him about the Island Line carriages
options.line: He warms up at once. Built 1938 for the Northern line, bought by the island in '89 because nothing else fits Ryde tunnel, and 'she'll do another fifty years if they let her.' He forgets to clip one of the tickets.
Sound recording, for a programme about seaside piers. He nods as if that is a thing that happens, and tells you Sandown's has the best penny falls on the south coast.

fail.line: 'Sound recording.' He writes something in a small book and the whole carriage watches him do it. Nobody says anything about it, which is worse.

man_with_ferret.title: A man with a ferret
man_with_ferret.text: A man in a flat cap gets on with a canvas bag that moves. He sits across from the party, opens the bag, and a ferret puts its head out and looks at Teddy. The man does not explain. Nobody else on the carriage looks up.

options.line: 'Rabbits,' he says, which is the whole answer. After a while he adds that there are rabbits on Culver Down like you would not believe, and that he will not go up there after dark, and that his dad would not either, and he was a hard man. The ferret goes back in the bag.

options.text: Let the ferret smell your hand
options.line: It is warm and quick and smells of straw, and it decides you are all right. The man nods as if you have passed something. 'She don't like everyone.' He gives you a name at the golf club to ask for.

fail.line: It bites. Not hard, but with intent. The man says 'She don't like everyone' and seems pleased about it, and the finger throbs all the way to Sandown.

options.line: The bag moves beside you for three stations and the man gets off at Brading with a nod. It is apparently the most normal thing that will happen all day.

tobacco_wagon.title: A tobacco wagon across the road
tobacco_wagon.text: A flatbed wagon stacked with speared tobacco, the sticks leaning like a haystack with a comb through it, has stalled crossways on the two-lane with a tractor in front of it and a man under the tractor. Two boys on the load look at the wagon the way people look at a parade float. There is no way round and no hurry anywhere in the county.

options.line: Four of you and the two boys and the wagon rolls far enough to let a car by. The man comes out from under the tractor with grease to the elbow and a jar of sweet tea from the cooler, which is the only pay he has. He says Kelly like it is just the next town, which it is.

options.text: Ask what's wrong with the tractor
options.line: A fuel line, sucked flat where it goes over the manifold. Teddy has the tape stock out before the man finishes the sentence, and the tractor starts on the second pull. 'You all from the government?' 'Sutton.' He thinks that over and tells you the Suttons on his mother's side saw the things in '55.

fail.line: You hand him tools for forty minutes while he says 'no, the other one' and the heat comes off the road in sheets. In the end it is a fuel line and his boy fixes it.

options.line: An hour on the shoulder with the windows down, listening to the cicadas and a boy on the load whistling the same four notes. The tractor catches eventually. The whistling stops before it does.

radar_trap.title: A radar trap outside Elizabethtown
radar_trap.text: A Kentucky State Police cruiser sits under an overpass with the radar gun resting on the mirror, where the parkway comes down a grade and everyone is doing seventy-five. The lights come on for the wagon. Out-of-state plates, antennas, a roof rack, and a trooper in a grey Stetson who takes his time walking up through the heat.

options.line: Investigators, Sutton, West Virginia, going to Hopkinsville on a case. He says 'Kelly' before you do, like a man naming a disease. He writes nothing, says the fair traffic on 41 is worse than any aliens, and watches you leave.

options.text: Tell him you're a film crew
options.line: Documentary, the Western Kentucky State Fair, public television. He asks which station and you say the one in Bowling Green. He has a cousin there. He loses interest and lets you go with a warning about the grade.

fail.line: He asks which station and you name a Louisville one that does not do documentaries. The ticket is for seventy-four in a sixty-five, the lecture is about honesty in the Commonwealth, and both take a while in the sun.

options.text: Kill the scanner before he reaches the window
options.line: The scanner goes dark a second before his hand finds the door. He looks at the box, then at you. 'Kentucky doesn't mind those,' he says, 'but Tennessee does,' and lets it go.

corvette_billboard.title: A billboard with a hole in it
corvette_billboard.text: NATIONAL CORVETTE MUSEUM, BOWLING GREEN, OPENING LABOR DAY, with a yellow '94 coupe painted eight feet long across it. Something has gone through the sign just behind the car's rear wheel: a hole the size of a dinner plate with the plywood splintered outward, as if whatever made it came from behind. Birds have been using it. The field behind the sign is nothing but cut hay.

options.line: Ruth walks the field behind the sign while the others wait in the shade of it. Nothing. No tracks, no shell, no stone. The hole is clean and the splinters all point toward the road. Teddy photographs it anyway, because the Office photographs things.

options.text: Ask at the gas station up the road
options.line: The man at the pump says it has been like that since June. 'Kids,' he says, and then, because you have not moved, 'well, somebody.' He gives you a map of Bowling Green with the museum on it and a cup of coffee that has been on the burner since dawn.
The yellow car and the hole go by. Somebody says it was probably a deer. Somebody else says deer do not hit things eight feet off the ground.

ohio_storm.title: A storm over the Ohio
ohio_storm.text: The thunderheads that have been standing over Ohio all day come across the river at once. The sky goes green, then black, and the bridge is suddenly a tunnel of water with the rails invisible and the wipers doing nothing. Lightning walks down the river. The radio is all static and under the static something that is not static.

options.text: Pull under the overpass and wait it out
options.line: Twenty minutes with the hazards on and the rain coming sideways, three trucks and a hearse waiting with you. It passes the way these things pass, all at once, and the river is steaming when you come out. The ones who get across fastest are the ones who sat still.

Twenty miles an hour with the window down to see the line, the river roaring under the deck and lightning close enough to smell. Then it is behind you and the sun is out on wet asphalt and the whole car breathes.

fail.line: Hydroplane, a long slow slide, the guardrail coming up and then not. The wagon stops crossways on the shoulder with everyone white. Nobody says anything for a mile.

options.line: Under the static, between the lightning crashes, three notes. Low, lower, a step up. Ruth reaches over and turns it off, and the storm goes on without it.

hitchhiking_soldier.title: A soldier with his thumb out
hitchhiking_soldier.text: A young man in BDUs with a duffel at his feet stands on the shoulder with his thumb out, not hopeful, just out, the 101st patch on his shoulder and a haircut that says he has been in the field a week. Fort Campbell is the direction you are going. He looks at the West Virginia plates like they are a flag from home.

options.line: He folds into the back with the duffel across his knees and talks for fifty miles, about Haiti maybe, about a sergeant, about a girl in Clarksville. Near Hopkinsville he goes quiet and says the post has a standing joke about Kelly, and the joke is that nobody from Charlie Company will take the 41 cutoff after dark, and it is not a joke.

options.text: Ask him about the post first
options.line: He says the division is on alert for somewhere hot and he would rather not say where. He says there are things the MPs log and things they do not, and gives you a name at the post gate and the number of a bar in Oak Grove. Then he takes the ride anyway and sleeps.

fail.line: He looks at the Office lettering on the door and decides you are reporters. The thumb comes down. 'Sir, I can't talk to the press,' he says, and means it.

options.line: He gets smaller in the mirror, standing very straight.

fireworks_stand.title: A fireworks stand with the flaps down
fireworks_stand.text: A plywood shed on the shoulder, FIREWORKS in red on every side, LAST CHANCE, the Fourth six weeks gone and the stock half price. A man in a lawn chair with a shotgun across his knees and a radio going. Mortar tubes, bottle rockets, Roman candles, and a box of the big ones with no label at all.

options.text: Buy a box of the big ones
options.line: Ten dollars for a box that would be illegal in three of the states you have driven through. The man says they are for scaring crows. 'Or whatever,' he says. The box goes in the back next to the tape stock, which nobody is happy about.

options.text: Ask what he's heard about Kelly
options.line: He turns the radio down. 'Every August,' he says. 'Every August somebody drives through asking.' He sells more Roman candles to Kelly folks in a week than to the rest of the county all summer, and he does not think it is for the Fourth.
The flaps go down behind you and the radio goes up.

loose_horse.title: A horse loose on the road
loose_horse.text: A horse stands in the middle of the Bluegrass road, a bay with a halter and no lead, looking back the way it came. The white fence runs unbroken on both sides for a mile and there is no gate open. It does not move for the wagon. Behind it, the field it should be in is empty, and the grass is flat in a circle wide enough to park in.

options.text: Walk it back to the fence
options.line: Ruth gets out slow with her hand low and the horse lets her take the halter. It walks with her to the fence and stands there shaking. The farm woman who comes down the lane in a truck says the gate has not been open since Tuesday and gives you a Thermos of coffee and a look that says she will be thinking about that for a while.

fail.line: The horse backs, wheels and goes down the road at a dead run, and keeps going. The farm woman who comes down the lane does not thank you. It takes an hour to find it and nobody mentions the circle in the grass to her.

options.line: Teddy gets the circle in the grass from the fence rail, three frames, before the horse decides to move on its own. It is probably a horse that rolled. It is a big horse. The circle is bigger.
Two wheels on the verge, the horse watching the car and not the road, and then it is behind you, still standing there, still looking back the way it came.

cantaloupe_man.title: A man selling cantaloupes
cantaloupe_man.text: A pickup backed into a church lot with a tailgate full of cantaloupes and a cardboard sign, 3 FOR $2. The man has a straw hat and a face that has done fifty summers of this. He waves the wagon in with the hat. Before the window is down he has seen the lettering on the door and has something to say.

options.text: Buy three and let him talk
options.line: 'My brother saw them,' he says, thumbing a melon. 'Fifty-five. He was eleven. Said they come across the field like they was walking on a floor you couldn't see.' He puts the cantaloupes in the car and will not take more than two dollars and will not say the brother's name. 'He don't want it in a book.'

options.text: Press him for the brother's name
options.line: He looks at the road and says a name, and a church, and that the brother is a deacon there and will deny it. He takes the two dollars and says the melons are a dollar extra for that, and they are.

fail.line: He puts the melon down. 'You all are the fourth this summer,' he says, and the hat comes off and the tailgate goes up and that is the end of the cantaloupes.

options.line: He waves the hat at the next car before you are out of the lot.

wsgb_1490.name: WSGB 1490 Sutton
wsgb_1490.text: Swap-and-shop and the Braxton County school closings, then the weather: nine degrees at the Sutton dam this morning, snow by evening below Charleston, the Elk running high under the ice. 'And a reminder from the sheriff's office: chains or good tread if you're headed down 35.'

wchs_580.name: WCHS 580 Charleston
wchs_580.text: '...news at the top of the hour. In Mason County, the Army Corps says the Point Pleasant floodwall will hold through the February thaw, though the Kanawha is running six feet above pool. And in Point Pleasant this week, residents mark the anniversary of the sightings of 1966 and '67 with a quiet that one councilman called, quote, well earned. Temperatures tonight in the teens with river fog along 35. WCHS, the voice of the Kanawha Valley.'

wvaf_999.name: WVAF V100 Charleston
wvaf_999.text: 'V100, Charleston's soft rock.' Mariah Carey's 'Hero' fades into Bryan Adams and the DJ reads a school delay list for Kanawha and Putnam in a voice built for selling mattresses. Then Celine Dion, 'The Power of Love', all the way to the county line.

wklc_1051.name: WKLC Rock 105 St. Albans
wklc_1051.text: 'Rock 105!' Pearl Jam's 'Daughter' straight into Nirvana's 'All Apologies', the DJ shouting over the outro about a Dollar Night at a bar in Nitro. In the back seat Teddy turns it up and Frank turns it down and nobody wins.

wqbe_975.name: WQBE 97.5 Charleston
wqbe_975.text: Country, loud and clear across the whole valley: Garth Brooks, 'The Red Strokes', then Alan Jackson's 'Chattahoochee' for the third time this winter. The farm report says the ground at Winfield is frozen fourteen inches down.

wvpn_885.name: WVPN 88.5 West Virginia Public Radio
wvpn_885.text: A woman reading the Mountain Stage schedule, then a feature on the Silver Bridge: a retired engineer explaining eyebar chains and a single cracked link in a voice so calm it is worse than shouting. 'Forty-six people. December 15th, 1967. The river was full of Christmas shopping.'

wbyg_1340.name: WBYG 1340 Point Pleasant
wbyg_1340.text: Faint and then clear as the river gets close: the Mason County obituaries, a Kroger ad, and a reminder that the riverfront lot is closed below the floodwall gate until the Kanawha drops. 'And if you see Carl's dog, she answers to Biscuit and she is not, whatever your neighbor told you, a wolf.' The Four Seasons, 'Walk Like a Man', 1963.

wjeh_990.name: WJEH 990 Gallipolis
wjeh_990.text: Across the river in Ohio, a man with a Gallia County accent reads the livestock prices and then a hospital board meeting, slowly, as if the whole county is writing it down. Between items, a thirty-year-old record: the Righteous Brothers, 'Unchained Melody', fighting the static all the way through.

wglp_937.name: WGLP 93.7 Gallipolis
wglp_937.text: Oldies off the Ohio side: the Shangri-Las, 'Leader of the Pack', the motorcycle crash and all, then a DJ who says his name is Captain Dave and that it is eleven degrees on the Gallipolis floodwall and dropping. 'Be careful on the Henderson bridge tonight, it's slick.'

wkee_1005.name: WKEE 100.5 Huntington
wkee_1005.text: Top 40 out of Huntington, strong until the hills eat it: Ace of Base, 'The Sign', Salt-N-Pepa, 'Whatta Man', and a car dealer on US-60 who will take anything on trade. 'Anything. Bring the dog.'

night_desk.name: The Night Desk, 1190 AM
night_desk.text: A clear-channel skip from somewhere flat and far: 'You're on the Night Desk, go ahead, caller.' A trucker from Ripley says he saw a man standing on the Henderson bridge railing at three in the morning, no coat, not cold, and when he came back the other way an hour later the man was still there and had not turned his head. The host says 'Mmhm' the way he says it to everyone, and takes a call about a dog that counts.

numbers_1.name: Unmarked, 1540 AM
numbers_1.text: A woman's voice, flat, a tone between each group: 'Four. Seven. Four. Zero. Two. Nine. Four. Seven. Four. Zero. Two. Nine.' Then a chime, then the same again. Nobody in the car says 'write that down', and somebody does.

numbers_2.name: Unmarked, 640 AM
numbers_2.text: A child's voice this time, or a woman doing one, in German by the numbers: 'Acht. Eins. Drei. Drei. Null. Sieben. Acht. Eins. Drei. Drei. Null. Sieben.' The signal rises and falls with the hills, and the last group comes through like it is sitting in the back seat.

tone.name: Between stations, 101.3 FM
tone.text: Nothing on 101.3, just hiss, and under the hiss, so faint the ear argues about it, three notes. Low, lower, then a step up. Again, slower, as if the thing making them is listening for an answer. The needle does not want to stay there. The signal meter says there is no signal at all.

radio_1_1053.name: BBC Radio 1, 1053 AM
radio_1_1053.text: Medium wave, which the BBC keeps promising to leave by July. 'And still at number one, for a second week, Manchester United and the Cup Final squad, Come On You Reds, with Wet Wet Wet breathing down their necks from that wedding film.' A jingle, a Bank Holiday traffic warning for the A3 to Portsmouth, and then Ace of Base, same as the hills at home.

radio_4_935.name: BBC Radio 4, 93.5 FM
radio_4_935.text: A calm voice reading a list to the whole country at a quarter to one in the morning. 'Wight, Portland, Plymouth. Southwest four or five, becoming variable three. Fair. Good, occasionally poor.' Then 'Sailing By', and then nothing at all until six. Nobody in the party knows what it was and everyone feels looked after.

ocean_fm_974.name: Ocean FM 97.4 Hampshire
ocean_fm_974.text: Hampshire's own: the Spice of Life, a Portsmouth car dealer, and the news. Bank Holiday queues on the M27, hovercraft running every half hour, 'and across the water, a Sandown story the Island paper is calling the Yellow Man: a golfer says a figure in a pointed hat crossed the links at dawn, and the club has nothing to say.' Then Take That.

iw_radio_1242.name: Isle of Wight Radio, 1242 AM
iw_radio_1242.text: The island's own, four years old and sounding like a village hall: a ferry delay at Yarmouth, the Sandown Carnival committee, a lost dog at Lake, and a presenter who says 'over on the mainland' as if it were abroad. 'And if you were on the Levels this morning and saw something, Sandown police would like a word. So would we, frankly.'

poacher.name: Unmarked, 1060 AM
poacher.text: Eight bars of a folk tune on something like a music box, over and over: a poacher, a moonlit night. Then a woman's voice, English, crisp as a newsreader: 'Two-four-one-nine-six. Two-four-one-nine-six.' Five figures at a time, each group twice, for ten minutes, then the tune again. Teddy says it is the Lincolnshire Poacher. Nobody asks how she knows.

callin_uk.name: Late Lines, 97.3 FM
callin_uk.text: A south coast phone-in after midnight, the host tired and kind. A woman from Shanklin says her husband saw lights over Culver Down in '73 and would not talk about it until the day he died, and then did, and the host lets the silence sit. A man from Gosport rings to say it was the Navy. 'It's always the Navy, Terry,' the host says. 'Next caller.'

whop_1230.name: WHOP 1230 Hopkinsville
whop_1230.text: '...WHOP news on the hour. The Western Kentucky State Fair opens its gates tonight at the fairgrounds on Richard Street with the tractor pull at seven, and Christian County marks another August 21st this weekend with a quiet the Chamber calls, quote, respectful. The Sutton family asks that visitors stay off the farm road. Dark-fired prices firm at the Pembroke warehouse. Ninety-four tomorrow, chance of storms after dark. WHOP, Hopkinsville, the Pennyrile's own.'

wkdz_1110.name: WKDZ 1110 Cadiz
wkdz_1110.text: The farm report, slow as the heat: 'Burley steady, dark-fired firm, feeder steers off a dollar at Guthrie. Corn's burning up in Trigg County and the Extension says don't bother with a second cutting. Lost: a bay gelding with a halter, Fairview road, call the number. Found: nothing yet. Hog futures after this from Ford of Cadiz.' Then a hymn, in full, because the next record is not cued.

whas_840.name: WHAS 840 Louisville
whas_840.text: Fifty thousand watts of clear channel from Louisville, strong as a station in the car: the Reds, if there are Reds tonight, the strike talk louder than the game. Between innings the host takes calls. A man from Oak Grove says the post has gone quiet and the buses are running at night, and a woman from Elkton says her dogs have not stopped since Monday. 'That's Christian County for you,' the host says, and goes to a break for a Louisville Chevy dealer.

fort_campbell_1600.name: Fort Campbell Post Information, 1600 AM
fort_campbell_1600.text: A loop on the top of the dial, a flat sergeant's voice over a hum: 'This is the Fort Campbell post information station. Gate 4 is closed to civilian traffic until further notice. Soldiers of the 101st Airborne Division, Air Assault, are reminded that the off-limits list has been updated; see your first sergeant. Range 41 is hot tonight. Civilians on US-41: expect convoy traffic after 2200. Do not stop for lights on the roadway. Repeat, do not stop for lights on the roadway.' Then the hum, then the loop again.

shortwave_preacher.name: Shortwave skip, 1570 AM
shortwave_preacher.text: A preacher bleeding in from the shortwave bands, somewhere in the Ozarks or on a mountain in Tennessee, the signal swelling and sinking like breathing: '...and they shall come up out of the earth, brother, and they shall have faces, and I'm telling you it has HAPPENED, it has happened in this country, in the state of Kentucky, in the year of our Lord nineteen and fifty-five, and the papers LAUGHED...' A card can be sent to a post office box in Nashville. The signal goes under and does not come back.

numbers_pennyrile.name: Unmarked, 1480 AM
numbers_pennyrile.text: A woman's voice, Southern, unhurried, as if reading a grocery list to someone she loves: 'Eight. Two. One. Five. Five. Eight. Two. One. Five. Five.' A tone between each group, a chime between each pair. Teddy says eight twenty-one fifty-five before anyone else does. The voice does not care. It says it again.
